abstract: In the mouse thalamus, thalamocortical neurons (TCNs) relay sensory information to cortex and generate rhythmic activity, including sleep spindles, through precisely timed firing. TCNs switch between tonic and burst firing modes that depend on intrinsic membrane properties, yet what maintains these properties in the mature thalamus remains unknown. Transcription factors, which regulate the ion channel genes that shape firing, are natural candidates. Here, we investigate Shox2, a transcription factor implicated in rhythmic activity across multiple systems, in ventral posterior medial (VPM) thalamus. Using genetic labeling and optogenetic activation, we show that Shox2 expressing neurons form functional thalamocortical and thalamoreticular projections capable of driving cortical responses. Conditional knockout of Shox2 in VPM alters intrinsic membrane properties, reducing both tonic and burst firing without altering thalamocortical circuit organization or barrel field architecture. These firing deficits are accompanied by impaired whisker-dependent somatomotor performance and a reduction in sleep spindle density in cortical target regions, while overall sleep architecture remains intact. Together, these findings identify Shox2 as a transcriptional regulator required to maintain intrinsic firing modes in VPM thalamocortical neurons, linking a transcription factor to spindle deficits, an emerging neurophysiological biomarker for autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia.
